The class name gives the mechanism: an aromatase inhibitor inhibits aromatase, "which means that you have to know what aromatase enzyme does" Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form, and aromatase makes estradiol; the drugs that block each enzyme, and the man without aromatase who grows tall with weak bones Thromboembolism, "the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens": estrogens raise clotting factors, and the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share the risk (his raloxifene dental case) The three anti-androgen classes: GnRH analogs (why a long-acting analog switches testosterone off), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride as Proscar and Propecia) and androgen receptor antagonists The SERMs by use: "tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid... to stimulate ovulation" Testosterone's adverse effects, with hepatotoxicity "the most important", and when to avoid it Emergency contraception: Plan B (levonorgestrel, within 72 hours, no prescription) versus ulipristal (a progestin receptor antagonist, up to 5 days, prescription only) 1 GnRH analogs: the body releases GnRH in pulses, but a long-acting analog (goserelin, leuprolide) stimulates the pituitary continuously until it switches off LH, FSH and testosterone; mainly prostate cancer; anti-sex-hormone side effects Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Long-acting GnRH analogs (goserelin) replace the natural pulses with constant stimulation, which shuts off FSH, LH and testosterone. The paradox: GnRH should be pro-androgen, because it drives LH and testosterone. The body releases it in pulses, a short burst and then a long pause with no release. These drugs are slow-release, long-acting analogs, so they stimulate the pituitary cells continuously, and eventually the cells switch off: FSH and LH secretion is suppressed, and with it testosterone. "That's the only way it's going to make sense to you": given this way, a GnRH analog works as an anti-androgen. 2 Blocking androgen metabolism and receptors: the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and dutasteride (Proscar and Propecia are one drug; his finasteride dental case) and the receptor antagonists flutamide and bicalutamide Study guide + recording + objectives · 4 questions in the bank Know this From Dr. Herr's study guide. For Dr. Fasinu's lecture that means each drug class by mechanism, use and main adverse effect: GnRH analogs (given continuously, they switch LH and testosterone off), the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride), the androgen receptor antagonists (flutamide, bicalutamide), the SERMs, aromatase inhibitors and progestins; how contraceptives work (progestins suppress FSH and LH, so no ovulation; Plan B versus ulipristal); and the adverse effects he stressed, thromboembolism for the estrogens and hepatotoxicity for testosterone. GnRH analogs Goserelin (Zoladex); also leuprolide (Lupron) Long-acting, continuous stimulation switches off FSH and LH, so testosterone falls Prostate cancer, BPH, precocious puberty, chemical castration Impotence, gynecomastia 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors Finasteride (Proscar, Propecia), dutasteride (Avodart) Block the conversion of testosterone to DHT BPH (higher strength), alopecia (lower strength) Gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction Androgen receptor antagonists Flutamide (Eulexin), bicalutamide (Casodex) Compete with testosterone at the androgen receptor Prostate cancer; excess androgens in women GI disturbances (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity 3 How hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy: progestins activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH and LH, so no ovulation; ethinyl estradiol in the combined pill; progestin-only pills (levonorgestrel) when estrogen is ruled out Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Mechanism: activation of the progestin receptor, which suppresses FSH (and LH and estradiol) secretion, preventing ovulation. 4 Thromboembolism, the estrogens' most serious side effect: more clotting factors and less antithrombin III; shared by the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors (his raloxifene dental case); any clot, even years ago, rules estrogen out Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Thromboembolism is estrogen's signature risk: a history of a clot rules estrogen out. A history of thromboembolism (a deep vein clot or a pulmonary embolism): avoid estrogen. "I think it's the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens," he said: estrogens disturb clot formation, so abnormal clotting is typical of estrogen therapy. 5 Testosterone's adverse effects and cautions: hepatotoxicity (the most important), virilization in women, feminization in men, lower HDL, and when to avoid it (BPH, pregnancy, breast cancer in men) Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): avoid testosterone, which fuels prostate enlargement. Women: hirsutism, including facial hair, a deepened voice, an enlarged clitoris and smaller breasts: the changes you expect in boys at puberty. These can be irreversible with prolonged use. Men: sleep apnea ("a big problem"), priapism, increased sex drive, and feminization: gynecomastia and azoospermia. He said the feminization is believed to come from testosterone being converted to estradiol. Both: acne, edema, hepatotoxicity, jaundice, lower HDL and higher LDL, dependence, aggressiveness and psychosis. 6 Emergency contraception: Plan B (levonorgestrel, 72 hours, no prescription) versus ulipristal (a progestin receptor antagonist, 5 days, prescription) Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Plan B: levonorgestrel, within 72 hours, no prescription. Ulipristal: an antagonist, up to 5 days, prescription only. Emergency contraception, side by side. Plan B is a high dose of levonorgestrel, a progestin; ulipristal is an antagonist: "The difference is this. This is an antagonist." Both have the same indication. The differences he called "probably more important": Plan B has to be used within 72 hours, while ulipristal can be used up to 120 hours, 5 days; and ulipristal is prescription only, while Plan B is sold without a prescription. 7 SERMs: tamoxifen (breast antagonist, uterine agonist, ER-positive tumors only), raloxifene for osteoporosis, clomiphene for ovulation Study guide + recording + objectives · 6 questions in the bank Know this Match each SERM to its use: tamoxifen, breast cancer; raloxifene, osteoporosis; clomiphene, ovulation. Clomiphene (Clomid) is used to induce ovulation: "kind of first-line drug for fertility." It is a weak agonist and strong antagonist at the estrogen receptors. By blocking them, it opposes the negative feedback of the body's own estrogen, so the LH and FSH pulses grow larger, and the ovary is driven to ovulate. It works in women whose hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is intact. How he read it: some, like tamoxifen, stimulate the uterus, and others don't; tamoxifen and raloxifene both act like estrogen on bone; none of them stimulates breast cells; and none of them inhibits ovulation. The same receptors are expressed at different levels in different cells, which is why the drugs have different uses: "So again, tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid, that is for, to stimulate ovulation." 8 Aromatase inhibitors: anastrozole blocks testosterone's conversion to estradiol to treat breast cancer; hot flashes and thromboembolism; not before menopause Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole): remember hot flashes and thromboembolism. Instead of blocking the estrogen receptor, you can stop estradiol from being made. Testosterone is aromatized to estradiol by aromatase, a natural enzyme, so an aromatase inhibitor inhibits the conversion of testosterone to estradiol. The most popular is anastrozole (Arimidex); letrozole (Femara) and exemestane (Aromasin) are the others. Use: breast cancer treatment. Adverse effects: hot flashes, GI disturbances, CNS disturbances (anxiety, confusion, depression) and thromboembolism. He said these drugs share estrogen-type side effects whether they act for or against estrogen: "At least you should be able to remember hot flashes... and thromboembolism." Contraindications: hepatic damage and premenopausal women. 9 Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form, and aromatase makes estradiol (the tall, osteoporotic man without aromatase) Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Estradiol closes the epiphyses, so a man without aromatase grows tall with weak, osteoporotic bones. The growth point is why aromatase deficiency matters. Estradiol is made from testosterone by aromatase, so a man born without aromatase cannot make estradiol, and his epiphyses don't close on time. "They're the ones that grow very tall": long bones, but weak, osteoporotic bones with a high risk of osteoporosis. His slide's treatment is estradiol. 10 What estrogen does and its side effects: female maturation and the endometrium, HDL and triglycerides up, bone protected; progesterone added to protect the uterus Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Female maturation: development of the vagina, uterus and secondary sex traits. Endometrium: growth of the uterine muscle and development of the uterine lining. His figure of estrogen as hormone therapy in menopause sets the good effects against the bad. Good: it strengthens bones, improves cholesterol (lower LDL, higher HDL) and reduces menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes. Bad: it increases the risk of breast cancer, of uterine cancer and of blood clots. The figure's footnote: the added uterine cancer risk can be reduced or eliminated by giving progesterone along with estrogen. 11 The estrogen drugs: estradiol from the ovary, ethinyl estradiol in oral contraceptives, and the indications Study guide + recording + objectives · 3 questions in the bank Estriol (E3), also made in the liver and peripheral tissues. The indications: primary hypogonadism in women (as testosterone is used in men), postmenopausal hormone therapy, oral contraceptives, suppressing ovulation in intractable dysmenorrhea or hirsutism, and fertility treatments. 12 How the sex steroids act (nuclear receptors) and what testosterone does (red cells, water retention, muscle); testosterone cypionate, the depot; progesterone matures the endometrium Study guide + objectives · 4 questions in the bank Erythropoiesis: it increases red blood cell formation, so androgens can treat refractory anemia. All the hormones in this block are very lipophilic, and they all bind nuclear receptors: thyroxine, the corticosteroids and the sex steroids alike. In the plasma they travel bound: the sex hormones to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), while a corticosteroid binds CBG. Only the free hormone reaches the receptor. Testosterone or DHT enters the cell and binds the androgen receptor (DHT is the main ligand, and testosterone binds it too), and the hormone-receptor complex changes gene expression. Because the effect goes through gene transcription, it takes time. Estradiol acts the same way through estrogen receptors. Also flagged in class Learn the examples in each class; the class name gives the mechanism, so know what each target enzyme or receptor does. 5-alpha-reductase bioactivates testosterone to DHT, so its inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) lower androgen activity. Hepatotoxicity is the testosterone side effect to know; liver disease is a contraindication. Proscar and Propecia are both finasteride: the higher strength treats BPH, the lower strength hair loss. Estrogens raise clotting factors 2, 7, 9 and 10, and the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share the clot risk. Tamoxifen is for ER-positive breast cancer only. Know the red drugs: goserelin, finasteride, dutasteride, flutamide, bicalutamide, tamoxifen, raloxifene, anastrozole, progesterone, hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel, ulipristal. You can skip Of the androgen drugs, know testosterone and testosterone cypionate (the IM depot); the other analogs on his table were not his focus. The rest of his second estrogen-effects slide (ACTH, well-being, binding globulins, FSH and LH inhibition) was skipped; know the clotting, lipid, bone, skin and uterine effects. Toremifene, ospemifene, bazedoxifene and fulvestrant on the SERM table are rarely used; know tamoxifen, raloxifene and clomiphene.
